item.title: Theory vs. Reality: Algorithms on Paper and in Practice
item.description:
Recently, in a blog post Yuval Domb describes a subtle, but remarkably clever optimisation that allows us to compute the montgomery product of two $n$ word1 integers using $2n^2 + 1$ multiplication operations. Although an improvement in theory, we were unable to manifest this speedup using the provided code. This post is a deep dive into why this could be?

Theoretical speedups promised by an algorithm often fail to materialize in real-world experiments. This is perhaps because a theoretical guarantee requires us to focus on a fixed set complexity metrics. For example, when we claim that Merge Sort is a faster sorting algorithm than Bubble Sort, what we really mean to say is it uses fewer comparison operations. In real world experimentation, faster usually means cpu cycles - which strongly depends on how said algorithm is implemented (and the hardware underneath). In what follows, we walk through a real-world case where a faster algorithm for Montgomery Multiplication does not immediately translate into practical speed.
